Using rpix with an IDE

Source: vignettes/articles/ide.qmd

Most R users work in an IDE rather than a terminal: RStudio, Positron or VS Code, or an editor such as Emacs, Neovim or Zed. Install the IDE as usual (see Installing the IDEs). Then let rpix point it at the R in your project’s Pixi environment, when you set the project up:

rpix::use_pixi(ide = "positron")

or later, for one IDE at a time, with use_pixi_rstudio(), use_pixi_positron(), use_pixi_vscode(), use_pixi_emacs(), use_pixi_neovim() or use_pixi_zed().

Some settings are a matter of taste, such as VS Code’s R console. rpix asks about them as it sets the IDE up. To answer in advance, e.g. in a script, give them as arguments, also to use_pixi():

rpix::use_pixi(ide = "vscode", console = "arf")

Whichever IDE you use, rpix::pixi_sitrep() checks that it runs the project’s R, and suggests fixes if it doesn’t.

Installing the IDEs

Install the IDE as you’d install any program. conda-forge has the command-line editors, and direnv, in recent versions, so Pixi can install them for you as your own tools, outside any project, with pixi global install:

IDE Install With Pixi
RStudio posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop
Positron positron.posit.co/download
VS Code code.visualstudio.com/download
Emacs gnu.org/software/emacs/download pixi global install emacs
Neovim neovim.io/doc/install pixi global install nvim
Zed zed.dev/download pixi global install zed
direnv, for Emacs, Neovim and Zed direnv.net/docs/installation pixi global install direnv
  • Neovim’s package is nvim. conda-forge’s neovim is its Python client, without the editor.
  • RStudio is on conda-forge too, as rstudio-desktop, but in a version from 2024; install it from Posit instead.
  • Commands: rpix’s setups for Emacs, Neovim and Zed, and for VS Code on Windows, say when the editor’s command (emacs, nvim, zed, code) isn’t on the PATH. An app can be installed without it: Zed’s comes from its zed: install cli command, and VS Code’s from Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH, on macOS. pixi global install puts the commands in ~/.pixi/bin, which is on the PATH.
  • direnv also needs hooking into your shell once, which pixi global install doesn’t do: see direnv’s instructions.

Positron

Set up 

rpix::use_pixi_positron()

This turns on Positron’s discovery of R in Pixi environments, and makes the R from the project’s default environment Positron’s default for the project, in .vscode/settings.json. default_r = FALSE leaves the default out.

Every day

Open the project, and Positron (2026.10 or later) starts its R. With an older Positron, or use_pixi_positron(default_r = FALSE), pick R (Pixi: default) in the interpreter picker once; Positron remembers it for the project. Either way, the environment is activated when R starts, on Windows too.

The default’s path is for the operating system use_pixi_positron() ran on. On another one, Positron ignores it, so collaborators there pick R (Pixi: default) once.

Another environment

Each of the project’s environments is listed as its own R, e.g. R 4.4.3 (Pixi: r44). Pick it in the interpreter picker, or run rpix::pixi_switch("r44"), which looks for interpreters again and opens the picker.

If something’s off

  • Positron starts another R. Positron prefers the R you last picked in the project over the default. If you used another R there before setting up Pixi, pick R (Pixi: default) once.
  • R (Pixi: default) isn’t listed. Positron may still show the R installations it found before, even in a new project. Run Interpreter: Discover All Interpreters from the Command Palette. Restart Positron if you’ve only just turned on discovery.

RStudio

Set up

For a new project, use RStudio’s File > New Project > New Directory > Project with Pixi. It does what use_pixi(ide = "rstudio") does, for the version of R you pick (4.5 by default: conda-forge has no R packages for R 4.6 yet), and makes the project a git repository if you ask.

For a project you have already, run in RStudio:

rpix::use_pixi(ide = "rstudio")   # or rpix::use_pixi_rstudio() in a Pixi project

This adds an rstudio task to pixi.toml, and creates an .Rproj file if the project doesn’t have one. Both ways need rpix in the R that RStudio runs.

RStudio also applies its own “Create a git repository” and “Use renv with this project” to templates, as you last left them in its New Project dialog, without showing them. renv clashes with Pixi, as both manage the project’s packages, so turn it off: run rstudioapi::writeRStudioPreference("new_proj_use_renv", FALSE) (or .rs.api.writeRStudioPreference(...) without rstudioapi), or create one project with it unticked. RStudio only saves the checkbox when a project is created, not when the dialog is cancelled. If renv got into a project, rpix says so, and that rpix::pixi_import_renv() turns it off.

Every day

Open the project in RStudio as usual, e.g. from its recent projects or by double-clicking the .Rproj file. RStudio picks its R when it starts, so it opens the project in your usual R. Once it’s ready, rpix asks:

? Reopen this project in a new RStudio, with its Pixi R?
1: Yes
2: No

Yes starts a new RStudio with the environment’s R, in the project, after installing the environment if it isn’t yet, and closes this one. Addins > Open with the project’s Pixi R, or rpix::pixi_switch(), does the same later. To stop the question, set RPIX_OFFER_SWITCH=false in your ~/.Renviron.

From a terminal, pixi run rstudio in the project folder starts RStudio with the environment’s R straight away. On Windows, the task expects RStudio in C:/Program Files/RStudio; if it’s somewhere else, change the path in pixi.toml.

Addins

rpix adds these to RStudio’s Addins menu:

  • Open with the project’s Pixi R: a new RStudio with the environment’s R (pick the environment if there are several).
  • Add packages…: the selected packages, or the code’s, or those you name.
  • Add the packages this file uses: those the active file uses and pixi.toml lacks.
  • Install the environment: e.g. after a git pull.
  • Run a task…: one of the project’s tasks.
  • Open pixi.toml.
  • Situation report: pixi_sitrep().

They’re there when rpix is installed in the R that RStudio runs. To give one a keyboard shortcut, use Tools > Modify Keyboard Shortcuts.

Another environment

From RStudio, run:

rpix::pixi_switch("r44")

This starts a new RStudio with the environment’s R, in the project. The first time, it can take a while to open. Close the old one when you’re done with it. Addins > Open with the project’s Pixi R does the same, and asks which environment.

From a terminal, pixi run --environment test rstudio works too, for environments that include the default feature, which the task belongs to.

If something’s off

  • RStudio uses another R, and rpix didn’t ask. rpix isn’t installed in the R that RStudio runs, so nothing can ask. Install it there, or use pixi run rstudio from a terminal.

VS Code

Set up 

rpix::use_pixi_vscode()

This adds the languageserver package to the environment, with the R extension’s sess (how it talks to R) and jgd (its plots), and points the R extension at the environment’s R, in the project’s .vscode/settings.json. It works the same in the editors based on VS Code, such as VSCodium, Cursor and Windsurf: they read the same settings, and get the R extension from Open VSX. A project set up once works in all of them.

sess and jgd aren’t on conda-forge yet, so they come from rpix-forge, a channel rpix adds to the project after conda-forge. The extension only uses a sess built from its own release, so when the extension is newer than rpix-forge’s sess, it offers to install its bundled copy: accept. It installs into a library of its own, and the packages sess needs are there already.

Another console

The R extension’s console can be arf or radian, instead of R. use_pixi_vscode() asks which, or takes it as an argument:

rpix::use_pixi_vscode(console = "arf")

This adds arf to the environment, and points r.consolePath at it, with r.consoleArgs telling it to start the environment’s R.

Every day

Open the project folder in VS Code. The R extension uses the environment’s R, and the project’s .Rprofile activates the environment.

On Windows, the environment’s R only starts when the environment is activated, because it needs the environment’s Library\bin folder on the PATH. So start VS Code from the project’s environment:

pixi run code .

For VSCodium, Cursor or Windsurf, use codium, cursor or windsurf instead of code.

Another environment

Run rpix::pixi_switch("r44"). It changes r.executablePath and r.consolePath in .vscode/settings.json to the environment’s R, ${workspaceFolder}/.pixi/envs/r44/bin/R. With arf or radian as the console, it keeps the default environment’s console, and points it at the environment’s R. Then run Developer: Reload Window from the Command Palette.

On Windows, start VS Code with pixi run --environment r44 code . instead (or codium, cursor or windsurf). The console then has to be in that environment too.

If something’s off

  • The R extension can’t find R. Check that the environment is installed (pixi install), and that the paths in .vscode/settings.json exist.
  • Positron and VS Code share .vscode/settings.json. Each ignores the other’s settings, so a project can be set up for both.

Emacs, Neovim and Zed

These editors start R, and languageserver, from the PATH. direnv puts the environment’s on it whenever you’re in the project’s folder.

Set up

Install direnv once (see Installing the IDEs), and hook it into your shell. Then, in the project:

rpix::use_pixi_emacs()   # or use_pixi_neovim(), use_pixi_zed()

This adds the languageserver package to the environment, and a .envrc file that activates the environment (rpix::use_pixi_direnv() writes just the file). direnv only loads a .envrc you’ve allowed, and again after it changes: rpix offers to allow it, or run direnv allow in the project.

Each editor loads direnv in its own way:

  • Emacs: install the envrc package and turn on (envrc-global-mode). ESS, and languageserver through eglot or lsp-mode, then use the project’s R.
  • Neovim: start Neovim from a shell with direnv’s hook, or use a direnv plugin such as direnv.vim. R.nvim and languageserver then use the project’s R.
  • Zed: Zed loads direnv by itself. Install its R extension: languageserver then uses the project’s R, and so does R in Zed’s terminal.

On Windows, direnv is rarely available, and the environment’s R only starts when the environment is activated. Start the editor from the environment instead: pixi run emacs, pixi run nvim or pixi run zed ..

Another environment

Run rpix::pixi_switch("r44"). It points .envrc at that environment. Reload direnv in the editor (in Emacs, M-x envrc-reload; in Neovim, start it again from the project; in Zed, reopen the project), then restart R.

The message at startup

If you start R in a Pixi project with an R that isn’t from the project’s environment, e.g. your usual R, the project’s .Rprofile says so, as long as rpix is installed in that R:

! This R isn't from the project's Pixi environment, so it doesn't use the project's packages.
ℹ Open the project in an IDE set up with `rpix::use_pixi(ide = ...)`, or start R with `pixi run R`. See https://roald-arboel.com/rpix/articles/ide.html.

In RStudio, it asks to reopen the project with the environment’s R instead (see RStudio).

Your usual R can’t use the environment’s packages: they’re built for the environment’s R, and loading them can crash another R. So rpix doesn’t try; start the environment’s R instead, as above.

Check

In the IDE’s R console, R.home() should be inside the project’s .pixi/envs/ folder:

R.home()
#> [1] "/path/to/project/.pixi/envs/default/lib/R"
